event-horizon-0aed8b33.title: Event Horizon (The Schwarzschild Metric)

\\( r_s \\).name: Schwarzschild Radius
\\( r_s \\).description: The radius defining the event horizon of a non-rotating, uncharged black hole. It is the distance from the center where the escape velocity equals the speed of light, and beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape.

\\( G \\).name: Gravitational Constant
\\( G \\).description: Newton's universal gravitational constant, a fundamental constant in physics that quantifies the strength of gravitational attraction between masses. Its approximate value is \( 6.674 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2 \text{ kg}^{-2} \).

\\( M \\).name: Mass of the Object
\\( M \\).description: The total mass of the celestial body or black hole for which the Schwarzschild radius is being calculated. This mass is assumed to be concentrated at a central point or within a spherically symmetric distribution.

\\( c \\).name: Speed of Light in Vacuum
\\( c \\).description: A fundamental physical constant representing the speed at which all electromagnetic radiation travels in a vacuum. It is the universal speed limit for the propagation of information and energy in the universe, with an approximate value of \( 2.998 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s} \).

\\(r\\).name: Radial Distance / Radius
\\(r\\).description: The radial distance from a central source or origin, typically used in spherical or cylindrical coordinate systems.

\\(s\\).name: Seconds / Proper Time Interval
\\(s\\).description: The SI unit of time, or the invariant interval traversed by a clock.

event-horizon-0aed8b33.interpretation: The formula \( r_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2} \) expresses a fundamental relationship in general relativity. The Schwarzschild radius \( r_s \) is directly proportional to the mass \( M \) of the object; larger masses have larger Schwarzschild radii. This means that more massive objects require less compression to form an event horizon, and their event horizons are larger. The gravitational constant \( G \) acts as a proportionality constant, quantifying the strength of gravity, while the speed of light squared \( c^2 \) in the denominator highlights the relativistic nature of the concept. The inverse square dependency on \( c \) shows that if light were slower, a less massive or less compact object could form a black hole, emphasizing the role of the ultimate speed limit in defining the event horizon.
event-horizon-0aed8b33.symmetry_origin: The Schwarzschild radius arises directly from the Schwarzschild metric, a solution to Einstein's field equations of general relativity. This metric describes the spacetime geometry around a spherically symmetric, non-rotating, uncharged mass distribution in a vacuum. The metric's singularity at \( r = r_s \) is not a true physical singularity (it's a coordinate singularity), but rather indicates the boundary of the event horizon, where the roles of radial and time coordinates swap, signifying that all future-directed paths inside this radius lead toward the central singularity.
event-horizon-0aed8b33.limits_and_boundary: As the mass \( M \) of an object approaches zero, the Schwarzschild radius \( r_s \) also approaches zero. This implies that for very small masses, the gravitational effects leading to an event horizon become negligible or require incredibly dense compression, far beyond what is naturally achievable for stable matter. Conversely, as \( M \) approaches infinity, \( r_s \) also approaches infinity, meaning extremely massive objects would have enormous event horizons. For typical celestial bodies like the Earth or the Sun, their Schwarzschild radii are tiny (e.g., Earth's \( r_s \) is about 9 mm, Sun's is about 3 km), far smaller than their actual physical radii, indicating that they are not black holes and their surfaces are well outside their theoretical event horizons. This formula essentially sets a boundary condition for when an object's self-gravity becomes dominant enough to trap light.
event-horizon-0aed8b33.conceptual_definition: The Schwarzschild radius, often denoted by \( r_s \), is a critical radius associated with any given mass \( M \). It represents the radius where, if all the mass \( M \) were compressed into a sphere of this radius or smaller, the escape velocity from its surface would equal the speed of light \( c \). For a non-rotating, uncharged black hole (a Schwarzschild black hole), this radius defines its event horizon, the boundary beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape the gravitational pull.
event-horizon-0aed8b33.intuitive_summary: The Schwarzschild radius quantifies how compact an object must be for its gravity to become so immense that light itself cannot escape, forming an event horizon.

instrumental-bias-7eda424d.title: Instrumental Bias

N_{obs}.name: Observed Number of Events
N_{obs}.description: The count of physical events, objects, or phenomena that have been successfully detected and recorded by a measurement instrument or during an observation period.

N_{true}.name: True Number of Events
N_{true}.description: The actual, underlying total number of events, objects, or phenomena that exist in the system being studied, irrespective of whether they were detected.

P(\\text{detect}).name: Probability of Detection
P(\\text{detect}).description: The likelihood, expressed as a number between 0 and 1, that any single event (from \( N_{true} \)) will be successfully detected and registered by the instrument. This probability often depends on the instrument's sensitivity, the signal strength of the event, and environmental conditions.

\\(N\\).name: Number of Particles / Normal Force
\\(N\\).description: The total count of atoms/molecules, or perpendicular contact force.

\\(P\\).name: Pressure
\\(P\\).description: The perpendicular force exerted per unit area on the boundary of a system.

\\(d\\).name: Total Differential
\\(d\\).description: Represents an infinitesimal change in a variable (e.g. dx, dt).

\\(e\\).name: Elementary Charge / Euler's Number
\\(e\\).description: The electric charge carried by a single proton, or the mathematical base of natural logarithms.

\\(t\\).name: Time
\\(t\\).description: The continuous, progressive sequence of events in which change occurs. It acts as the independent variable in dynamical equations of motion.

\\(c\\).name: Speed of Light
\\(c\\).description: The maximum speed at which all conventional matter and information in the universe can travel.

instrumental-bias-7eda424d.interpretation: The equation establishes a fundamental relationship between the observed count, the true underlying count, and the efficiency of the detection process. Here, \( N_{obs} \) represents the number of events or objects that an observer or instrument actually registers. This value is what is directly measured in an experiment or observation. \( N_{true} \) signifies the actual, underlying number of events or objects that exist in reality, some of which might not be detectable by the instrument. The core of the instrumental bias is captured by \( P(\text{detect}) \), which is the probability (a value between 0 and 1, inclusive) that any single event, if present, will be successfully detected. If \( P(\text{detect}) = 1 \), the instrument is perfectly efficient, and \( N_{obs} = N_{true} \). However, if \( P(\text{detect}) < 1 \), then \( N_{obs} \) will always be less than \( N_{true} \), indicating that some events went unobserved due to the instrument's limitations or experimental conditions. This implies that to infer \( N_{true} \) from \( N_{obs} \), one must accurately determine \( P(\text{detect}) \).
instrumental-bias-7eda424d.symmetry_origin: This formula originates from the foundational principles of probability theory and statistical sampling, rather than from a fundamental physical symmetry or conservation law. It describes a statistical relationship in observational measurement processes. It is a direct consequence of treating detection as a Bernoulli trial for each potential event, where the aggregate observed count is the sum of these trials, scaled by the true number of events.
instrumental-bias-7eda424d.limits_and_boundary: 1. If \( P(\text{detect}) = 1 \) (perfect detection efficiency), then \( N_{obs} = N_{true} \), indicating no instrumental bias and a complete census of events. 2. If \( P(\text{detect}) = 0 \) (zero detection efficiency), then \( N_{obs} = 0 \), meaning no events are observed regardless of how many truly exist. 3. If \( N_{true} = 0 \) (no true events), then \( N_{obs} = 0 \) for any \( P(\text{detect}) \), as nothing can be observed if it doesn't exist. 4. As \( P(\text{detect}) \) approaches 0 from above (e.g., \( P(\text{detect}) \to \epsilon \) for small \( \epsilon > 0 \)), then \( N_{obs} \to N_{true} \cdot \epsilon \), indicating that very few events will be observed even if many exist. 5. As \( P(\text{detect}) \) approaches 1 from below (e.g., \( P(\text{detect}) \to 1 - \epsilon \) for small \( \epsilon > 0 \)), then \( N_{obs} \to N_{true} \cdot (1 - \epsilon) \), meaning almost all events are observed.
instrumental-bias-7eda424d.conceptual_definition: Instrumental bias, in the context of observational science, refers to the systematic deviation between the true underlying number of physical events or objects and the number that are actually observed or detected by an instrument or survey. This bias arises because no detector is perfectly efficient, meaning there is always a probability less than one that an existing event will be successfully recorded. The formula quantifies this relationship, showing that the observed count is directly proportional to the true count, with the constant of proportionality being the detection probability.
instrumental-bias-7eda424d.intuitive_summary: The number of events actually observed by an instrument is the true total number of events scaled by the instrument's probability of successfully detecting each one.

electromagnetism-5ad10a96.title: Electromagnetism

\\( \\mathbf{E}_{\\perp}' \\).name: Perpendicular Electric Field in Moving Frame
\\( \\mathbf{E}_{\\perp}' \\).description: The component of the electric field in the moving inertial frame that is perpendicular to the relative velocity \( \mathbf{v} \).

\\( \\mathbf{E}_{\\perp} \\).name: Perpendicular Electric Field in Stationary Frame
\\( \\mathbf{E}_{\\perp} \\).description: The component of the electric field in the stationary inertial frame that is perpendicular to the relative velocity \( \mathbf{v} \).

\\( \\gamma \\).name: Lorentz Factor
\\( \\gamma \\).description: A factor that accounts for relativistic effects, defined as \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} \), where \( v \) is the relative speed and \( c \) is the speed of light.

\\( \\mathbf{v} \\).name: Relative Velocity
\\( \\mathbf{v} \\).description: The constant velocity of the moving inertial frame relative to the stationary inertial frame.

\\( \\mathbf{B} \\).name: Magnetic Field
\\( \\mathbf{B} \\).description: The magnetic field vector in the stationary inertial frame.

\\(E\\).name: Electric Field Strength
\\(E\\).description: The magnitude of the electric field vector, representing the force per unit charge at a point in space.

\\(x\\).name: Position / Displacement
\\(x\\).description: A coordinate representing the location of a particle along a specific axis, or the displacement from an equilibrium position.

\\(v\\).name: Speed / Velocity Magnitude
\\(v\\).description: The rate of change of position with respect to time, representing the speed of a particle.

\\(B\\).name: Magnetic Field Strength
\\(B\\).description: The magnetic flux density representing electromagnetic field induction.

electromagnetism-5ad10a96.interpretation: The equation relates the electric field component perpendicular to the relative velocity in a moving frame, denoted by \( \mathbf{E}_{\perp}' \), to the electric and magnetic fields measured in a stationary frame. \( \mathbf{E}_{\perp} \) is the component of the electric field in the stationary frame that is perpendicular to the relative velocity \( \mathbf{v} \). \( \mathbf{B} \) is the magnetic field in the stationary frame. The term \( \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \) represents an electric field that arises in the moving frame due to the interaction of its velocity with the magnetic field present in the stationary frame. This is a crucial relativistic effect: a purely magnetic field in one frame can contribute to an electric field in a frame moving relative to it. The Lorentz factor \( \gamma \) accounts for time dilation and length contraction effects inherent to special relativity, ensuring that the transformation is consistent with the constant speed of light. The transformation of the parallel component of the electric field is simpler: \( \mathbf{E}_{\parallel}' = \mathbf{E}_{\parallel} \).
electromagnetism-5ad10a96.symmetry_origin: This transformation law is a direct consequence of the Lorentz invariance of Maxwell's equations and the transformation properties of the electromagnetic field tensor \( F^{\mu\nu} \). The electromagnetic field tensor combines the electric and magnetic fields into a single relativistic entity. The principles of special relativity, particularly the constancy of the speed of light in all inertial frames and the relativity principle (physical laws are the same in all inertial frames), necessitate these specific transformation rules for the electric and magnetic fields to maintain the covariance of Maxwell's equations under Lorentz transformations.
electromagnetism-5ad10a96.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit, as \( v \ll c \) (where \( c \) is the speed of light), the Lorentz factor \( \gamma \) approaches 1. In this case, the equation simplifies to \( \mathbf{E}_{\perp}' \approx \mathbf{E}_{\perp} + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \). This approximation highlights how a moving observer perceives an additional electric field \( \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \) due to their motion through a magnetic field, which is fundamental to concepts like motional electromotive force. As \( v \to c \), the Lorentz factor \( \gamma \) approaches infinity. If the term \( (\mathbf{E}_{\perp} + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \) is non-zero, the perpendicular electric field \( \mathbf{E}_{\perp}' \) in the moving frame would become infinitely large, signifying the strong relativistic compression of fields and energy density for observers approaching the speed of light relative to a source.
electromagnetism-5ad10a96.conceptual_definition: This formula describes how the electric field component perpendicular to the relative velocity between two inertial frames transforms under special relativity. It demonstrates the interwoven nature of electric and magnetic fields, showing that what appears as an electric field in one frame can be a mix of electric and magnetic fields in another moving frame.
electromagnetism-5ad10a96.intuitive_summary: Electric and magnetic fields are not independent but rather different manifestations of a single electromagnetic field, transforming into each other for observers in relative motion.

geometric-duality-86a9761a.title: Geometric Duality (Covariant Vectors (One-Forms))

V_\\mu.name: Covariant Vector Components
V_\\mu.description: The components of the covariant vector (one-form), which transform under coordinate transformations in a manner opposite to contravariant vectors.

\\eta_{\\mu\\nu}.name: Minkowski Metric Tensor
\\eta_{\\mu\\nu}.description: The flat spacetime metric tensor with signature usually defined as (-1, 1, 1, 1) or (1, -1, -1, -1), defining the geometric structure of special relativity.

V^\\nu.name: Contravariant Vector Components
V^\\nu.description: The components of the original contravariant vector, transforming in the same manner as coordinate differentials.

\\(V\\).name: Electric Potential
\\(V\\).description: The amount of work energy needed to move a unit of electric charge from a reference point to a specific point in an electric field.

\\(\\mu\\).name: Reduced Mass / Permeability / Friction Coefficient
\\(\\mu\\).description: Effective inertial mass in two-body problems, magnetic field capability, or surface grip factor.

\\(\\eta\\).name: Efficiency / Viscosity / Minkowski Metric
\\(\\eta\\).description: Ratio of useful work output to input energy, fluid shear resistance, or flat spacetime metric.

\\(\\nu\\).name: Kinematic Viscosity
\\(\\nu\\).description: The ratio of dynamic viscosity to density, representing a fluid's resistance to shear flow under gravity.

geometric-duality-86a9761a.interpretation:
In this equation, \(V^
u\) represents the contravariant components of a vector, geometrically visualized as an arrow or tangent vector. The Minkowski metric tensor \(\eta_{\mu
u}\) represents the geometric structure of flat spacetime. By performing a tensor contraction over the index \(
u\) (using Einstein summation convention), the metric maps the contravariant vector to its dual covariant counterpart \(V_\mu\). Covariant vectors, or one-forms, are geometrically interpreted as a series of parallel, oriented hypersurfaces that measure how many times a vector pierces them, acting as linear functionals on the vector space.
geometric-duality-86a9761a.symmetry_origin: The duality is rooted in the algebraic properties of inner product spaces. In physics, its invariant nature is a consequence of Lorentz covariance in special relativity, ensuring that the contraction of covariant and contravariant vectors yields coordinate-independent scalar invariants (such as spacetime intervals or physical actions).
geometric-duality-86a9761a.limits_and_boundary: In flat Euclidean space, the metric tensor reduces to the Kronecker delta \(\delta_{ij}\), meaning there is no distinction between covariant and contravariant components (\(V_i = V^i\)). In general relativity, when gravity or curvilinear coordinates are introduced, the constant Minkowski metric \(\eta_{\mu\nu}\) generalizes to the coordinate-dependent metric tensor \(g_{\mu\nu}\), though the index-lowering mechanism remains structurally identical.
geometric-duality-86a9761a.conceptual_definition: This formula describes the index-lowering operation in relativistic physics and differential geometry. It represents the canonical isomorphism (often referred to as the musical isomorphism 'flat', \(\flat\)) between the tangent space (contravariant vectors) and the cotangent space (covariant vectors or one-forms) of flat Minkowski spacetime, mediated by the metric tensor \(\eta_{\mu\nu}\).
geometric-duality-86a9761a.intuitive_summary: The metric tensor acts as a geometric translator, converting directional tangent vectors into measurement-oriented one-forms by lowering their indices.

point-source-response-6a0a64e1.title: Point-Source Response

\\(\\Phi\\).name: Electrostatic Potential
\\(\\Phi\\).description: A scalar field representing the amount of potential energy per unit charge at a given location in an electric field. The electric field is the negative gradient of the electrostatic potential.

\\(\\rho\\).name: Charge Density
\\(\\rho\\).description: The amount of electric charge per unit volume at a specific point in space. It is the source of the electrostatic potential.

\\(\\varepsilon_0\\).name: Vacuum Permittivity
\\(\\varepsilon_0\\).description: A fundamental physical constant representing the ability of a vacuum to permit electric field lines or, equivalently, its capacity to store electric energy. It relates electric fields to their sources in free space.

\\(\\epsilon_0\\).name: Vacuum Permittivity
\\(\\epsilon_0\\).description: The capability of the vacuum to permit electric field lines.

\\(P\\).name: Pressure
\\(P\\).description: The perpendicular force exerted per unit area on the boundary of a system.

\\(o\\).name: Origin / Offset
\\(o\\).description: The starting point of a coordinate system, or baseline shift.

\\(i\\).name: Imaginary Unit
\\(i\\).description: The mathematical constant defined by the property i² = -1 (sometimes written as j).

\\(s\\).name: Seconds / Proper Time Interval
\\(s\\).description: The SI unit of time, or the invariant interval traversed by a clock.

\\(n\\).name: Refractive Index / Particle Density
\\(n\\).description: The ratio of speed of light in vacuum to that in a medium, or particles per unit volume.

point-source-response-6a0a64e1.interpretation:
The equation 
                
                    \(\nabla^2 \Phi = -\rho / \varepsilon_0\)
                
                describes how a scalar potential field, 
                
                    \(\Phi\)
                
                , is influenced by a source distribution, 
                
                    \(\rho\)
                
                . The term 
                
                    \(\nabla^2\)
                
                is the Laplacian operator, which measures the local 'curvature' or 'concavity' of the potential field 
                
                    \(\Phi\)
                
                . A negative Laplacian (i.e., 
                
                    \(\nabla^2 \Phi < 0\)
                
                ) indicates a local maximum in potential, while a positive Laplacian (
                
                    \(\nabla^2 \Phi > 0\)
                
                ) indicates a local minimum. The charge density 
                
                    \(\rho\)
                
                represents the volume density of electric charge, acting as the 'source' or 'sink' of the potential. A positive charge density 
                
                    \(\rho > 0\)
                
                results in a negative Laplacian for 
                
                    \(\Phi\)
                
                , meaning positive charges are associated with potential 'sinks' (local minima if the potential is defined to be positive for positive charges). The constant 
                
                    \(\varepsilon_0\)
                
                , the vacuum permittivity, scales the relationship between charge and potential in a vacuum. It is a measure of how well a vacuum permits electric field lines.
point-source-response-6a0a64e1.limits_and_boundary:
In regions where there is no net charge, i.e., 
                
                    \(\rho = 0\)
                
                , Poisson's equation reduces to Laplace's equation: 
                
                    \(\nabla^2 \Phi = 0\)
                
                . Solutions to Laplace's equation are called harmonic functions, describing potentials in charge-free regions. For a single point charge 
                
                    \(q\)
                
                located at the origin, the charge density is given by 
                
                    \(\rho(\mathbf{r}) = q\delta(\mathbf{r})\)
                
                , where 
                
                    \(\delta(\mathbf{r})\)
                
                is the Dirac delta function. The solution to Poisson's equation for a point charge is the well-known Coulomb potential: 
                
                    \(\Phi(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\)
                
                , which also represents the 'point-source response' or Green's function for the Laplacian operator. As the distance 
                
                    \(r\)
                
                from a localized charge distribution approaches infinity, the potential 
                
                    \(\Phi\)
                
                typically approaches zero. The specific solution to Poisson's equation depends on the boundary conditions, such as Dirichlet boundary conditions (where 
                
                    \(\Phi\)
                
                is specified on the boundary) or Neumann boundary conditions (where the normal derivative of 
                
                    \(\Phi\)
                
                is specified on the boundary).
point-source-response-6a0a64e1.conceptual_definition:
Poisson's equation is a second-order partial differential equation that relates the electrostatic potential 
                    
                        \(\Phi\)
                    
                    to the charge density 
                    
                        \(\rho\)
                    
                    that creates it. It is a fundamental equation in electrostatics, serving as a generalization of Gauss's Law in differential form, and is crucial for calculating electric fields and potentials arising from arbitrary charge distributions.
point-source-response-6a0a64e1.intuitive_summary: The curvature of the electrostatic potential at any point is directly proportional to the local charge density at that point, with a negative sign indicating that positive charges create 'dips' in the potential field.

sterile-particle-da8bdb51.title: Sterile particle

\\mathcal{L}.name: Lagrangian Density
\\mathcal{L}.description: The spatial density of the Lagrangian, containing the kinetic and interaction terms of the fields.

y_{\\nu}.name: Neutrino Yukawa Coupling

\\nu_R.name: Right-handed Sterile Neutrino
\\nu_R.description: The right-handed Weyl spinor field representing the sterile neutrino, which does not participate in weak, electromagnetic, or strong interactions.

M_R.name: Majorana Mass Matrix
M_R.description: The high-energy mass scale matrix representing the explicit lepton-number-violating mass of the right-handed sterile neutrinos.

C.name: Charge Conjugation Matrix
C.description: The Dirac matrix acting on spinor fields to transform a particle into its antiparticle.

\\(\\nu\\).name: Kinematic Viscosity
\\(\\nu\\).description: The ratio of dynamic viscosity to density, representing a fluid's resistance to shear flow under gravity.

\\(y\\).name: Position Coordinate
